newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UNHCR boss - world lost interest in Zaire refugees.
newsitem.headline: UNHCR boss - world lost interest in Zaire refugees.

text.p: The U.N. refugee chief Sadako Ogata criticised the international community on Tuesday for losing interest in the plight of hundreds of thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees still trapped in a war zone in eastern Zaire.

Speaking ahead of a tour of Africa's troubled Great Lakes region starting on Thursday, Ogata said the world had breathed a collective sigh of relief when 600,000 Hutus went home after rebels overran their camps, but she added that up to 400,000 were still in eastern Zaire.
"We have to help these people. We can't let them just wither away," she told Reuters in an interview.
"To reach the refugees, our people cross rivers, trek in mountains or use bikes. I don't think you can carry goods by bicycle but this is the way we've been working," she said.
"It hasn't been an easy one. We really need international support. But I don't see very active international support. All this time, the world has lost interest in these refugees."
The main hurdle to aid distribution was the lack of security guarantees and humanitarian corridors, Ogata said.
Western countries led by the United States abandoned the idea of the force after most of around 1.1 million Rwandan Hutu refugees in Zaire returned home after rebel victories in 1996.
But renewed warfare between rebels and Zaire's army backed by European mercenaries has again turned the focus on refugees.
Ogata said the world's reluctance to send in troops to separate the refugees from militia had complicated the crisis.
"At the high-point of the exodus, if a large force came in to demobilise and separate the refugees, it would have saved a lot of security problems later on," she said.
Now the main priority is to stop the refugees from being caught in the middle of fighting, she said. "I appeal that there will be no attacks on the refugees, that they would be spared."
"The refugees are between the frontlines. How can you help them from whatever fighting that's going to take place very soon? It's going to be very difficult. There's a war."

Reports from the region say Tutsi-led rebels are pushing closer towards the Lubutu area, where 200,000 refugees are camped out in three camps -- Tingi-Tingi (120,000), Amisi (40,000) and Shabunda (40,000).
Despite the fighting, Ogata ruled out evacuation of UNHCR's staff from the region. "We have plans for deployment right now, not evacuation," she said. "The situation in the camps is bad."
The UNHCR said on Tuesday the refugees were down to only a week of U.N. food suppplies and that they were dying at a rate of 20 a day from malnutrition and disease in Tingi-Tingi.

Ogata spoke at length on Monday with Emma Bonino, the Eruopean Union commissioner who described conditions at Zaire's largest remaining refugee camp for Hutus as beneath human dignity and said the international community should be ashamed.
"They agreed on the need for political action to help the humanitarian agencies carry out their work on the ground," a UNHCR spokeswoman said.
Ogata's week-long tour of the region will take her to Zaire's capital Kinshasa and Tingo-Tingi in the east as well as Rwanda, Burundi, Uganda and Tanzania.
In Kinshasa, Ogata said she may also meet President Mobutu Sese Seko, who is stricken with prostate cancer and was absent from his vast, anarchic country during much of the rebellion.
Mobutu, who was convalescing in France from cancer surgery, is in Morocco for talks with his long-time ally King Hassan and will fly to Kinshasa on Thursday, officials said.
